turn_text: Chris, pleasure to be with you again. Look, the Constitution divided power between the branches of government on purpose. The framers had just fought a brutal eight-year war against a king. Concentrated authority. And they didn't want a king, they didn't want a monarch, they didn't want a dictator. And they realized that if you put all the power into one set of hands, it's just dangerous. The ancient principle is power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely. And they were trying to deal with that fundamental issue by putting certain powers in the Congress and certain powers in the presidency. In fact, in Article 2, they severely limited the powers of the President because, again, they were afraid of a king, of a monarch. The President does have the power as Commander-in-Chief in time of war, but interestingly, they even split that power and gave the power to declare war to Congress. There was quite a debate at the Constitutional Convention in August of 1787 about the war power and they split it because they didn't want a president running off and starting a war on his or her own. Now, the other piece was, who makes laws? And they gave the power to make laws to the Congress And in article two, the president's responsibility, not power, but responsibility, and this is an exact quote, is to take care that the laws be faithfully executed. It doesn't say make your own laws, decide which laws you like, enforce some and not others. It says, take care that the laws, all laws, be faithfully executed. Again, why did they do this? Not because they wanted to create a clumsy system just for fun or it was just somebody's Madison's weird idea. It was to purposefully keep power out of the hands of one person or one institution. That's where we're in trouble right now. because the actions of this administration have clearly crossed that line to take the power of legislation from the Congress to the president, closing AID. I'm sorry, AID was created by statute. It was a statute of Congress signed by the president, I think, and I can't remember, 1998. And to say, we don't like AID, we're going to close it down, is a straight up violation of a law passed by Congress and the president taking it unto himself to make those kinds of decisions.
